title: 07. Advanced & Agentic RAG: Building Your First MCP Server (Raw Python SDK)
summary: In previous lessons we learned about Tools, Resources, and Prompts using FastMCP. Today we use the raw MCP Python SDK — the lower-level approach — so you understand exactly what happens under the hood.
objectives: ① Real-World Analogy — Building with Bricks vs a Pre-fab Kit
⑤ Complete Code Example — Calculator Server (Raw SDK)
⑥ Testing with the MCP Inspector

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: **In previous lessons** we learned about Tools, Resources, and Prompts using FastMCP. **Today** we use the **raw MCP Python SDK** — the lower-level approach — so you understand exactly what happens under the hood.

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy — Building with Bricks vs a Pre-fab Kit
sections.body:
Imagine building a house. You can:

1. **Bricks approach (raw SDK):** Buy individual bricks, cement, tools. You assemble everything yourself. More work, but you understand exactly how every wall is built.

2. **Pre-fab kit approach (FastMCP):** Buy a kit where walls are pre-made. Much faster, but the inner details are hidden.

In this lesson we use **bricks** (the raw SDK). In Lesson 8 we switch to the **pre-fab kit** (FastMCP). Understanding the bricks first makes you a much better builder, even when you use the kit.

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
The **MCP Python SDK** (`pip install mcp`) is the official, lower-level library. With it, you manually:
- Create a `Server` object
- Register handlers for `list_tools`, `call_tool`, `list_resources`, etc.
- Handle the JSON-RPC message routing yourself (or let the SDK handle it)
- Start the server with a transport

It is more code than FastMCP, but you see exactly what MCP does at every step.

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body: When you hit a bug in FastMCP (Lesson 8), you will need to know what FastMCP is doing underneath. If your FastMCP server returns unexpected data, you need to know "what JSON structure does MCP actually expect?" — and the raw SDK makes that very visible. Also, some advanced MCP features are only available through the raw SDK.

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
### The Raw SDK Approach Flow

```
Step 1: Import Server and types from mcp.server
Step 2: Create a Server(name) instance
Step 3: Register a @server.list_tools() handler
        → This tells the SDK "when client asks for tool list, call THIS function"
        → Returns a list of Tool objects with name, description, inputSchema

Step 4: Register a @server.call_tool() handler
        → This tells the SDK "when client calls a tool, call THIS function"
        → Receives: tool name + arguments dict
        → Returns: list of content objects

Step 5: Run the server with a transport runner
        → stdio: use stdio_server() context manager
```

sections.title: ⑤ Complete Code Example — Calculator Server (Raw SDK)
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- When a client asks "what tools do you have?", this function runs and returns our tool list.
- When a client calls a tool, this function runs.
- Main function that starts the server.
- A complete calculator MCP server using the RAW MCP Python SDK
- Install: pip install mcp
- STEP 1: Create the server
- Give your server a name — this is what clients will see
- STEP 2: Register the "list tools" handler

**Defines:** `handle_list_tools()`, `handle_call_tool()`, `main()`

```python
# calculator_raw_sdk.py
# A complete calculator MCP server using the RAW MCP Python SDK
# Install: pip install mcp
# Run:     python calculator_raw_sdk.py

import asyncio              # Python's async library — MCP uses async throughout
import sys                  # For stderr logging (NEVER print to stdout in stdio mode!)
from mcp.server import Server                # The core MCP server class
from mcp.server.models import InitializationOptions   # Server startup options
from mcp.server.stdio import stdio_server            # stdio transport runner
from mcp import types                                # MCP type definitions

# ─── STEP 1: Create the server ────────────────────────────────────────

# Give your server a name — this is what clients will see
server = Server("calculator-server")

# ─── STEP 2: Register the "list tools" handler ────────────────────────

@server.list_tools()           # This decorator registers the handler
async def handle_list_tools() -> list[types.Tool]:
    """
    When a client asks "what tools do you have?",
    this function runs and returns our tool list.
    
    We must describe EACH tool with:
    - name:        the identifier the client uses to call the tool
    - description: what the tool does (AI reads this!)
    - inputSchema: the JSON Schema for the tool's inputs
    """
    print("Client asked for tool list", file=sys.stderr)  # Log to stderr (NOT stdout!)
    
    return [
        types.Tool(
            name="add",                    # Tool identifier
            description="Add two numbers together and return the sum. Use this when the user wants to add, sum, or find the total of two numbers.",
            inputSchema={                  # JSON Schema for inputs
                "type": "object",          # Always "object" for tool inputs
                "properties": {            # Define each input field
                    "a": {
                        "type": "number",  # Can be integer or decimal
                        "description": "The first number to add"
                    },
                    "b": {
                        "type": "number",
                        "description": "The second number to add"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["a", "b"]    # Both inputs are mandatory
            }
        ),
        types.Tool(
            name="subtract",
            description="Subtract the second number from the first. Use when the user wants to find a difference or subtract.",
            inputSchema={
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "a": {"type": "number", "description": "The number to subtract from"},
                    "b": {"type": "number", "description": "The number to subtract"}
                },
                "required": ["a", "b"]
            }
        ),
        types.Tool(
            name="multiply",
            description="Multiply two numbers together. Use when the user wants a product or to multiply.",
            inputSchema={
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "a": {"type": "number", "description": "The first number"},
                    "b": {"type": "number", "description": "The second number"}
                },
                "required": ["a", "b"]
            }
        ),
        types.Tool(
            name="divide",
            description="Divide the first number by the second. Returns an error if dividing by zero.",
            inputSchema={
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "a": {"type": "number", "description": "The dividend (number to divide)"},
                    "b": {"type": "number", "description": "The divisor (number to divide by) — must not be zero"}
                },
                "required": ["a", "b"]
            }
        ),
    ]

# ─── STEP 3: Register the "call tool" handler ─────────────────────────

@server.call_tool()            # Registers the handler for tool calls
async def handle_call_tool(
    name: str,                 # Which tool the client wants to call
    arguments: dict            # The arguments the client provided
) -> list[types.TextContent | types.ImageContent | types.EmbeddedResource]:
    """
    When a client calls a tool, this function runs.
    
    name:      The tool name (e.g., "add")
    arguments: Dict of arguments (e.g., {"a": 5, "b": 3})
    
    Must return a list of content objects — usually TextContent.
    """
    print(f"Tool called: {name} with arguments {arguments}", file=sys.stderr)
    
    # ── Route to the right handler based on tool name ──────────────
    
    if name == "add":
        # Extract arguments — use .get() with type conversion for safety
        a = float(arguments.get("a", 0))   # .get() avoids KeyError if missing
        b = float(arguments.get("b", 0))
        result = a + b
        # Return as a list containing one TextContent object
        return [types.TextContent(type="text", text=str(result))]
    
    elif name == "subtract":
        a = float(arguments.get("a", 0))
        b = float(arguments.get("b", 0))
        result = a - b
        return [types.TextContent(type="text", text=str(result))]
    
    elif name == "multiply":
        a = float(arguments.get("a", 0))
        b = float(arguments.get("b", 0))
        result = a * b
        return [types.TextContent(type="text", text=str(result))]
    
    elif name == "divide":
        a = float(arguments.get("a", 0))
        b = float(arguments.get("b", 0))
        
        # ALWAYS validate before operating
        if b == 0:
            # For errors, we raise McpError
            raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero. Please provide a non-zero divisor.")
        
        result = a / b
        return [types.TextContent(type="text", text=str(round(result, 10)))]
    
    else:
        # Tool name not recognized — this should not happen if list_tools is correct
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool: '{name}'. Available tools: add, subtract, multiply, divide")

# ─── STEP 4: Run the server ───────────────────────────────────────────

async def main():
    """
    Main function that starts the server.
    We use stdio_server() which handles the stdin/stdout transport.
    """
    print("Calculator MCP Server starting...", file=sys.stderr)
    
    # stdio_server() is an async context manager that:
    # 1. Sets up stdin/stdout as the transport
    # 2. Returns (read_stream, write_stream) for the server to use
    async with stdio_server() as (read_stream, write_stream):
        
        # server.run() is the main loop — it:
        # 1. Reads JSON-RPC messages from read_stream
        # 2. Routes them to our registered handlers
        # 3. Writes responses to write_stream
        await server.run(
            read_stream,
            write_stream,
            InitializationOptions(
                server_name="calculator-server",     # Identifies our server
                server_version="1.0.0",              # Our server version
                capabilities=server.get_capabilities(  # What we support
                    notification_options=None,
                    experimental_capabilities={}
                )
            )
        )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # asyncio.run() starts the async event loop and runs our main() function
    asyncio.run(main())
```

sections.title: ⑥ Testing with the MCP Inspector
sections.body:
The **MCP Inspector** is a web-based tool for testing MCP servers without writing a client.

```bash
# Install MCP Inspector (it's an npx tool — needs Node.js)
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python calculator_raw_sdk.py

# This will:
# 1. Start your Python server
# 2. Open a web browser with a UI for testing
# 3. Let you click buttons to call tools and see results
```

sections.title: ⑦ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
```
❌ Mistake 1: Using print() instead of print(..., file=sys.stderr)
   Why it happens: Reflex from non-MCP Python development
   ✅ Fix: In stdio mode, stdout IS the MCP channel. Any stray print()
         will inject garbage into the JSON-RPC stream and crash the server.
         ALWAYS use: print("debug message", file=sys.stderr)

❌ Mistake 2: Returning a string instead of list[TextContent]
   Example: return "8"  instead of  return [TextContent(type="text", text="8")]
   Why it happens: Forgetting the required return structure
   ✅ Fix: Tool handlers MUST return a list of content objects.
         The list can have one item: [TextContent(type="text", text=str(result))]

❌ Mistake 3: Forgetting async/await
   Example: def handle_call_tool(name, args):  (not async!)
   Why it happens: Forgetting that MCP handlers are async
   ✅ Fix: ALL handlers registered with @server.list_tools(), @server.call_tool(),
         etc. MUST be async functions (defined with "async def").

❌ Mistake 4: Not handling unknown tool names in call_tool
   Why it happens: Assuming only valid tool names will come in
   ✅ Fix: Always have an "else" clause that raises a ValueError with
         a helpful message listing the valid tool names.

❌ Mistake 5: Calling asyncio.run(main()) inside a Jupyter notebook
   Why it happens: Jupyter already has an event loop running
   ✅ Fix: In Jupyter, use: await main()  (not asyncio.run(main()))
         Or use nest_asyncio: import nest_asyncio; nest_asyncio.apply()
```

sections.title: ⑧ Quick Recap — What Did We Just Learn?
sections.body:
- ✅ Raw SDK = more code, but you see exactly what MCP does at every level
- ✅ `list_tools()` handler → returns Tool objects with name, description, schema
- ✅ `call_tool()` handler → receives (name, arguments), returns `[TextContent(...)]`
- ✅ NEVER `print()` to stdout in stdio mode — use `file=sys.stderr`
- ✅ ALL MCP handlers must be `async def` functions
